title: CSS selectors and cascade
runtime: Modern evergreen browser. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript fragments can be tried in a small local page or the browser DevTools described in the lesson.

objectives.text: Choose simple selectors that match the intended elements.
Predict a winning declaration using origin, importance, specificity, and source order.
Prefer reusable classes and avoid specificity fights.

learningFlow: Apply it to a fresh page

diagnostic.question: What does .card select?
diagnostic.answer: Every element whose class list contains card.

sections.title: Read a CSS rule
sections.body: In .card { color: navy; }, .card is the selector, color is the property, and navy is the value. The declaration sits inside the rule block. A selector matches elements; it does not change the HTML structure.

sections.title: Start with simple selectors
sections.body: A type selector such as button matches a tag. .primary matches a class, #checkout matches one document ID, [disabled] matches an attribute, and :focus-visible matches a state. Combine selectors only when the relationship matters. Classes are usually the easiest reusable styling hook.

sections.title: Use combinators for real relationships
sections.body: A space selects descendants, > selects direct children, + selects the next sibling, and ~ selects later siblings. A long selector tied to many DOM levels breaks easily when markup changes. Prefer a direct class when the style belongs to a component.

sections.title: How a conflict is decided
sections.body: The browser first considers relevant declarations and cascade origin and importance. Within the winning origin and layer, specificity decides stronger matches. If specificity is equal, the later declaration wins. Inheritance supplies some values such as color to descendants when no declaration overrides them.

sections.title: Specificity is a comparison, not a target score
sections.body: Inline styles, IDs, classes or attributes or pseudo-classes, and types or pseudo-elements contribute at different levels. Do not keep adding selectors or !important to win. Inspect the competing rule and simplify the design. :where() is useful when a selector should add no specificity.

sections.title: Class names remain normal CSS
sections.body: In JSX you write className, but the browser receives a class attribute and applies normal CSS rules. React does not isolate selectors automatically. CSS Modules, naming systems, or layers can reduce collisions later.

practice.prompt: For <button class="save primary">, which selectors match: button, .save, #save, [class], and a?

acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.

solution.explanation: button, .save, and [class] match. #save does not because there is no id, and a targets another element type.

solution.explanation: Inspect the element, locate all declarations for the property, identify why one wins, then reduce or reorganize specificity. Use !important only for a deliberate cascade policy, not as a reflex.

interviewQuestions.question: How does the browser decide which CSS declaration wins?
interviewQuestions.answer: It filters relevant rules, considers cascade origin and importance, then layers, specificity, scoping proximity where relevant, and source order for remaining ties.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Why is “the most specific selector always wins” incomplete?

interviewQuestions.question: Why can !important make a codebase harder to maintain?
interviewQuestions.answer: It jumps to the important cascade and often starts another priority fight. Later overrides may need even more deliberate importance and origin handling.

interviewQuestions.question: What is CSS inheritance?
interviewQuestions.answer: Some computed property values, such as color, flow from a parent to descendants when they have no winning value of their own. Many layout properties do not inherit.
interviewQuestions.followUp: How is inheritance different from a descendant selector?

commonMistakes.symptom: A style is crossed out in DevTools
commonMistakes.cause: Another matching declaration wins the cascade.
commonMistakes.fix: Inspect origin, importance, layer, specificity, and source order instead of adding !important immediately.

commonMistakes.symptom: A selector stops working after harmless markup changes
commonMistakes.cause: It depends on a long descendant path.
commonMistakes.fix: Add a component class to the actual styling target.

commonMistakes.symptom: Many unrelated elements share an ID selector
commonMistakes.cause: IDs must be unique and create strong specificity.
commonMistakes.fix: Use a reusable class for repeated visual styles.
